articles.title: AI photos are making it harder to know what you're booking on Airbnb. Here's what to look out for
articles.summary: Josh Wells was excited to explore Montreal on his first trip outside the U.S. But as he scrolled through listings on Airbnb, he noticed something odd: Several host profile pictures and one listing…

image.caption: Josh Wells noticed that text on an artwork in an Airbnb listing looked jumbled, which raised his suspicions that the image had been edited or generated using AI. (Josh Wells/Reddit)

blocks.text: LISTEN | When Airbnb photos don't match reality:
Cost of Living5:19Can you believe what you see on Airbnb?

Josh Wells, a college student from Iowa, was excited to explore Montreal on his first trip outside the U.S. But as he scrolled through Airbnb listings in search of a place to stay, he began to notice something that didn't seem quite right.
Several of the hosts renting out their properties had profile pictures that Wells suspected were generated by artificial intelligence.
"Your average person taking an iPhone photo, there's obviously like a little bit of imperfections," Wells told the CBC's Cost of Living. "The AI photos, they just looked too perfect."
Still, Wells kept browsing. He was even close to booking one of the properties when a final look at the listing's photos raised another red flag.

He zoomed in on a piece of wall art depicting two halves of faces joined together. At the top, the artwork appeared to read "Picasso." But in another photo of the same room, taken from a different angle, the artwork looked different.
"The text was all warped and funky," he said. "I'm just like, 'Yeah, OK, this is AI."

When booking his trip to Montreal, Wells found extremely polished-looking photos of hosts appeared in numerous Airbnb listings, leading him to suspect they had been generated using AI. Short-term rentals in that city are subject to strict rules aimed in part at protecting the city's housing supply. (Josh Wells/Reddit)

That was enough to put Wells off the listing — and ultimately using Airbnb for this trip. Unable to tell whether the photos showed a real place or an AI-generated version of one, he opted for an apartment-style hotel instead.
"The fake profile picture is one thing, but listings of the actual place that you're staying at and spending thousands of dollars was an immediate no for me," Wells said.
Wells isn't the only traveller to question whether the photos found on Airbnb or similar short-term rental-style platforms accurately reflect reality.

items: Why some travellers are falling out of love with Airbnb

blocks.text: In July, an Ottawa family reported that their daughter arrived at a Toronto Airbnb to find a room that looked significantly different from the listing photos, which they suspected had been generated or heavily altered using AI.

The family provided side-by-side photos showing differences in the room and bathroom. Airbnb said the listing did not match the property and refunded the guest, but did not confirm whether artificial intelligence had been used.

As AI makes it easier to alter photos, experts say travellers may find it increasingly difficult to know whether Airbnb-style listings accurately reflect reality, raising questions about consumer trust and protections in Canada.
When a photo makeover goes too far

The proliferation of free, quick and easy-to-use AI tools is making photo editing increasingly tempting, said Francis Syms, associate dean in the faculty of applied sciences and technology at Humber Polytechnic in Toronto.

Beyond the major AI platforms, such as ChatGPT, Claude by Anthropic and Google's Gemini, countless other websites offer free tools for modifying images, said Syms. Hugging Face, for example, hosts thousands of AI tools that let users upload and edit photos.

"In a matter of 10 seconds, you can upload a picture to one of these sites and ask it to remove all the smudges or to change the furniture," he said. "You'll get that image back maybe 30 to 60 seconds later."
Artificial intelligence platforms like ChatGPT allows users to quickly and easily edit photos. (Marco Bertorello/AFP via Getty Images)
It's difficult to know where AI editing crosses into deception, said Daniel Guttentag, an associate professor of hospitality and tourism management at the College of Charleston in South Carolina.

"If you put in a fake hot tub on the back patio, I think basically everyone would agree that that is a blatant misrepresentation of what one's unit offers," he said. "Whereas if you just start to play with the lighting a little bit … I think most people would be comfortable with that.
"But then there's a whole lot of space in between, when it crosses that line into, 'Wait, this isn't what I signed up for.'"
Guttentag said another concern is the use of AI-edited images to make it appear that guests have damaged a property, potentially leading to compensation claims.
In 2025, a guest from London, U.K., booked an Airbnb in Manhattan and was accused of causing more than £12,000 ($22, 665) in damage.
She disputed the claim after noticing inconsistencies in photos of a supposedly cracked coffee table, which she suspected had been digitally manipulated or generated by AI.
Airbnb initially said she owed more than £5,000 ($9,444), but later fully refunded her after the case drew media attention.
Can you trust what you see online?
Relying on listing photos to decide which property to book makes trust particularly important for Airbnb guests, said Guttentag.
"You can't try it on in advance, like a pair of shoes," he said. "You have to have the confidence and the trust that it's going to live up to your expectations."

Although AI-altered photos might help hosts attract bookings in the short term, guests who arrive to find something different than what was advertised may leave negative reviews, Guttentag said. If people feel misled "one too many times," he said, it could prompt them to stop using the platform altogether.

Daniel Guttentag is an associate professor of hospitality and tourism management at the College of Charleston in South Carolina with research interests in Airbnb and artificial intelligence. (Submitted by Daniel Guttentag)

In a statement to CBC News, Airbnb says its rules require listings to be "accurately represented" and that the company may ask hosts to remove content that uses AI or other digital technology to "edit flaws, hide damage, add amenities or attributes that are not part of a listing, or otherwise materially misrepresent the listing."

The company further said it encourages guests to report misleading listings and that those who find a property that doesn't match its description can contact its 24/7 community support team. Under AirCover, Airbnb added, it may help guests find a similar place or provide a refund if the host can't resolve the issue.

In August, California's Artificial Intelligence Transparency Act (CAITA) took effect, requiring AI-generated images, videos and audio to carry information that can help consumers identify whether digital content was created or altered using AI.

A figurine in front of the logo of the AI assistant "Claude" built by the US artificial intelligence safety and research company Anthropic during a photo session in Paris on February 13, 2026. (Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images)

Canada doesn't yet have AI-specific legislation addressing misleading advertising, said Steve Szentesi, a Toronto-based competition and advertising lawyer. But he said existing laws can already apply to deceptive AI-generated images.

The federal Competition Act prohibits misleading advertising, whether the claims are made through text, photos, audio or other forms of media. Provincial and territorial consumer protection laws offer similar safeguards.

While AI-generated images are relatively novel, the underlying issue is not, Szentesi said. Courts have dealt with disputes over real estate listings for decades, including cases where photos of a property didn’t match the home itself or contradicted descriptions in the listing.

For consumers who believe a short-term rental listing misrepresents a property, Szentesi suggests first raising it with the rental platform. They can also file a complaint with the Competition Bureau or their provincial or territorial consumer protection act.

items: AI 'slop' is dominating menus, as some restaurant owners turn to it to save time and money
Can I get AI face? Plastic surgeons say AI-generated inspiration is more than meets the eye

blocks.text: In the meantime, Syms suggests would-be bookers look for possible signs of AI-generated images in listing photos, such as crooked door frames, tile lines and countertops, oddly shaped furniture, inconsistent shadows or reflections, and blurry or jumbled words on books or wall art.
Travellers can also use a tool like Google Lens, he said, to search for the same image online and check whether it has been taken from another website rather than showing the actual property.

For Wells, the experience hasn't ruled out him using Airbnb altogether — he had a positive experience booking with the platform in Kansas City in March. But his search for a place in Montreal has made him more wary, he said.
"I am open to it again as long as there's just no fake AI listings involved."

articles.title: I don't know many committed separatists. But I know people who are angry and hungry for change
articles.summary: Matthew Morin is a Calgary resident who is drawn toward Alberta separatism because daily life feels more precarious and he feels those on top don’t seem to care.

image.caption: Matthew Morin lives in Calgary and spends his free time hiking in the nearby Rocky Mountains. He says the experience of precarity in daily life influences his views on separatism. (Submitted by Matthew Morin)

blocks.text: Calgary·First Person
Matthew Morin is a Calgary resident who is drawn toward Alberta separatism because daily life feels more precarious and he feels those on top don’t seem to care.
The feeling that life is now precarious shapes my view of independence
· for CBC First Person
· Posted: Oct 10, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 6 hours ago

This First Person column is the experience of Matthew Morin, who lives in Calgary. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ. Also, check out our series on the Alberta referendum here and learn how we selected the writers.
After work on a recent evening, I was waiting for the C-train on 8th Street in downtown Calgary, right by the convenience store we locally call Crack Macs.
Off to one side, I saw a woman slumped from a likely overdose while her friend pushed the Narcan dispenser up her nose. To my left, two police officers were handcuffing another woman on the cement.
A few minutes later, a man asked me if I was selling side (slang for methamphetamine). Apparently I looked like a drug dealer to him. But, I mean, in this economy, who wouldn’t be, right?
As I was about to board the train, I looked up and on the TV screens at the station as a written news announcement rolled by: StatsCan publishes data showing violent crime is down.
I chuckled. Welcome to the world of hypernormalization — where systems are broken, statistics don't reflect the lived reality and politicians carry on as if it's acceptable.

items: Should Alberta separate? Here's why these Canadians feel the way they do

blocks.text: This is what is shaping my view of Alberta independence — the feeling that life is now precarious and those in charge don’t seem to care.

Downtown Calgary wasn’t like this when I used to come for a night out as a young man in the 2010s. And it’s not just the state of downtown. Friends looking for work aren’t getting interviews. Meat and fresh vegetables have become careful purchases for those in my circle. Plans to buy a home have quietly died for a lot of people I know.

I see it at my work in the health sector where we sometimes talk about the lack of resources for the vulnerable — shelters at capacity, waitlists for programs that were once quick to access, programs underfunded and stretched beyond capacity, a drug and mental health crisismismanaged by political and corporate entities.
It feels like they have left us — regular Canadians and Albertans — to manage the disarray.

When I first heard separatism being discussed, it was in the context of getting more of a voice for Alberta. Premier Danielle Smith was pitching her Sovereignty Within a United Canada Act and I thought that might be enough to quell that discontent and that it would provide Albertans a greater sense of control over their future.
But I was wrong. The discontent is larger than I first thought, and Smith and the federal government’s actions over the last three years haven’t improved life here on the ground.
Now when I think about the anger I feel and see around me, I think the rupture began even earlier, during COVID.

For me, it wasn’t about whether the rules were important or not. It was about how they were implemented and enforced. The dystopian experience of having to show vaccine passports, people getting in trouble for ice skating, the federal government freezing Convoy protesters’ bank accounts, closing small businesses while big-box stores stayed open, and seeing politicians dining together on a rooftop as if they’re exempt from their own rules — these rules made me realize how little political capital the average citizen actually holds.

In a video widely shared on social media in December 2020, Calgary police are shown telling a man to leave the ice. When he refuses, he is eventually taken to the ground by officers. Despite signage posted at the site, police said more than 40 people were using the outdoor rink — breaking gathering restrictions intended to prevent the spread of COVID-19. (Facebook)

Since then, the world has gotten more volatile. When politicians on both sides focus on pronouns and book bans, all the -isms, more DEI or less DEI, all the culture war issues that most people are exhausted by — it just seems tone deaf.

This is on both the federal and provincial governments. They can insist this is a “vibecession,” not a recession. They can announce that immigration is “under control,” that crime rates are stable, that tens of thousands of jobs were added, that GDP is up or that a pipeline might get built. None of that matters when a single tomato at the till costs $2.50 or broccoli is $3.99/pound, the neighbourhood feels less safe and that our wages aren’t keeping up.

Most people I know aren’t separatists; most people I know are angry. The line between those two groups gets blurred. And when I’m ticked off at the situation and it feels like no one in power actually cares, I feel the urge to look for a new solution, even if it’s radical.
But of course, I’m not about to just vote in anger.

As the debate over separation grew, I started to follow the separatist leaders on social media and watch their public comments. Some of this leaned into the conspiratorial: allegations of Chinese communist plots in Canada or of election fraud. There was a post, since taken down, that mocked Calgary’s mayor as too flamboyant, and others saying that Canada should have accepted the trade deal with the U.S.
The social commentary feels exclusionary, especially as a gay man myself, and the choice to align with the U.S. felt more 51st state adjacent rather than pro-Alberta.

Not all the leaders are like this. Keith Wilson articulates separatist thinking in a way that I can sometimes nod along with, especially when he’s talking about the material struggles of Albertans and the economic case for independence.
Keith Wilson, leader of independence group Let Alberta Decide. (Jennifer Chevalier/CBC)
But overall, these posts make me skeptical. I’m not sure I trust most of the separatist leaders to actually lead this movement.

I don’t know what will happen on Oct. 19. We might see a strong showing for separation simply as a protest vote. But I’ll bet even a strong showing for the remain side is not going to end talk of Alberta independence; the anger here is far larger than the people willing to entertain the idea of separation.
People are looking for hope, and when I’m standing in downtown Calgary, watching all this misery around me, I’m looking for hope, too.

articles.title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?
articles.summary: The Pentagon says the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, but experts suggest officials are reading the country wrong.

blocks.text: They came in their thousands from near and far - men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.

It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heat wave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to the spectators.
By the execution time of 5am, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.
That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.
The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.

Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner;" the local sheriff had died four months earlier, and his widow became the unlikely female replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.
That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in America. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky, and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.

By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.

A little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.
The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad would be live-streamed.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.
University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked.
"I never imagined [another] public execution," he told BBC.
He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining; it was 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%.
"It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said.
It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's nearly certain that millions or more will tune in.
With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment … bring your popcorn, invite your friends".
Sonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream.

"What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up … to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific."

Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's 2002 death, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap.
The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution.

"I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific."
But the polarisation and rhetoric in American politics may have, in some way, perhaps set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University.

"Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't, and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution; they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'"

articles.title: ‘Like a drill going into my eye’: why the mystery over Havana syndrome refuses to die
articles.summary: Dozens of CIA officers have been afflicted by debilitating symptoms over the past decade. Are they the result of ‘mass hysteria’? Or are they from attacks with an energy weapon and, if so, who is…

blocks.text: Shortly after 1am one night in April 2019, a CIA officer on a work trip to London was jolted awake in his hotel room by the most intense head pain he had ever experienced. His body was soaked with sweat and he felt like his eyes were spinning in their sockets. He manoeuvred his way out of bed, hoping to make it to the bathroom to vomit, but found his sense of balance had deserted him. Eventually, he fell back into a fitful, shallow sleep.

The next day, arriving at the work meeting he had travelled for, the officer found he could not remember the names of colleagues in the room, people he knew well. As the meeting got under way, he could barely follow the discussion. Initially, he chalked it up to a terrible – if rather odd – case of food poisoning. But over subsequent weeks, worrying symptoms persisted: brain fog, loss of balance and increasingly harsh tinnitus.

By September, he had started to feel better and was on another work trip, this time to Poland. Asleep in his Warsaw hotel room, he was again woken by terrifying head pain, even worse than in London. He later described the sensation as “someone standing over me with a baseball bat and just repeatedly hitting me on the head”. It was a nine or 10 on the pain scale, he felt, worse than anything he could remember.

Two hours later, the same feeling returned, and he started to suspect that what was happening might not be an internal process but rather some external attack. He dragged himself off the bed and curled up on the floor, where the intense pain subsided somewhat. That was the last time he had the “attack” sensation, but he went on to suffer chronic nerve pain, fatigue and other severe health problems for years.

blocks.caption: The incidents acquired the name Havana syndrome after the Cuban city where mass reports of the phenomenon first emerged. Photograph: Manon Levet/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Sources described the man in question as a senior CIA officer who had recently been assigned an important job relating to worldwide operations against Russia. At the time, he was only vaguely aware of the stories that had emerged from Cuba two years previously, about US diplomats who believed they may have been attacked with a sonic weapon.

These incidents, in which people reported feeling a variety of unusual sounds, pressure and pain, followed by residual symptoms that could last for years, had acquired the name Havana syndrome, after the city where mass reports of the phenomenon first emerged.

Later, dozens of CIA officers around the world reported Havana syndrome episodes, which in official documents were called anomalous health incidents (AHIs). Many believed AHIs were the result of a Russian intelligence operation to wound or intimidate covert US operatives using a previously unknown weapon that delivered sonic or pulsed microwave energy.

There was sustained pushback against that theory. Some scientists insisted the idea of a portable weapon that could deliver these injuries belonged in the realm of science fiction. They said a whole range of conditions could cause pain, dizziness and cognitive issues.

Various experts suggested AHIs could be down to environmental factors, toxins or even the sound of chirping crickets. One explanation was that the symptoms were psychogenic and the result of “mass hysteria”, while some inside the CIA even accused those involved of faking their injuries in the hope of a medical payout. The disagreements over what was causing Havana syndrome led to bitter arguments and broken friendships at the spy agency.
In 2022, a panel of scientific experts convened by the US government concluded that “the signs and symptoms of AHIs are genuine and compelling” and “could be due to external stimuli”.

But the next year, a long-awaited report delivered the official assessment of the US intelligence community: “The available intelligence consistently points against the involvement of US adversaries in causing the reported incidents,” read an unclassified summary. It was “very unlikely” that a sinister Russian campaign was behind AHIs, it concluded.

Yet the mystery of Havana syndrome refuses to die. This summer, the “very unlikely” assessment from 2023 was rescinded by Donald Trump’s outgoing director of national intelligence, who claimed it was based on flawed analysis.

Now, a decade after the first reports emerged from Havana, two CBS journalists who have covered the story from the start are to release a book that sets out the case for Russia being behind at least some of the episodes. It also accuses parts of the US government and intelligence community of covering up the evidence.
This article is based on early access to their findings, as well as on the Guardian’s own interviews with intelligence sources, AHI patients and scientists.

David Relman, the Stanford professor who led the official scientific panel on Havana syndrome in 2022, told the Guardian he believed there was a subset of AHI cases that were “most plausibly explained by exposure to pulsed microwave energy”.

His panel had access to patient records and to more than 1,000 classified documents on the topic. “To any reasonable person looking at all the evidence I was able to see, it inevitably leads to the conclusion that there may have been a cover-up,” he said.

Michael Rey and Oriana Zill de Granados are longstanding producers for the CBS programme 60 Minutes. In an interview at the programme’s studios in midtown Manhattan, the pair recounted how they first came across the story a decade ago.

They covered the Obama administration’s policy of re-establishing diplomatic relations with Cuba in 2015, so when reports emerged the next year of a mysterious new condition afflicting employees at the reopened embassy in Havana, they contacted a senior US diplomat who had been posted there. “I expected him to say: ‘This is all bullshit,’” said Zill. “But he said: ‘Oh no, this is completely true. And I can put you in touch with a bunch of people who were hit.’”

The pair spoke to more than a dozen of them, off the record, but by the time they were ready to put a story together there were new reports of similar cases occurring among US diplomats stationed in China. Then there were whispers about it happening in other locations around the world.

blocks.caption: Oriana Zill de Granados and Michael Rey, producers for 60 Minutes and authors of the forthcoming book The Havana Syndrome. Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The Guardian

blocks.text: Once the first 60 Minutes episodes devoted to the topic aired, victims started contacting the producers, keen to tell their stories. Many of these new sources were – or had been – undercover operatives for the CIA, meaning they could not speak openly as most details of their work were classified. But people stationed around the world who had not known each other told stories that seemed remarkably similar.
A pattern linked some of the key cases: the alleged victims were working, or had previously worked, on beats where they rubbed up against Russian interests.

In some cases, the location of the supposed hits was notable in itself: allies of Moscow where some part of the elite was looking to improve relations with the west. This was the case in Cuba, where the original cluster of cases had come during the Obama-era thaw in relations with the US, which had irritated hardliners in the Cuban regime and their backers in Moscow.

It was also the case in Georgia, Kyrgyzstan, Serbia and Vietnam. Several CIA officers who had been stationed in Kyiv around the time of the 2014 Maidan revolution in Ukraine, decried by the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, as a US-backed coup, later suffered AHIs in different locations across the world.

“I went through years of doubts about the story, and all the crazy things we were hearing,” said Zill. But the more source meetings she and Rey had, the more they felt there really was something there. “We’re meeting these highly effective intelligence officers and they’re all telling versions of the same story,” said Rey.

The origins of Havana syndrome go back long before Cuba. A cornerstone case is that of Mike Beck, a counter-intelligence officer at the National Security Agency who got sick while on temporary assignment to an undisclosed location in the 1990s to check a US diplomatic facility for bugs.

Beck developed a rare form of Parkinson’s disease at the age of 45 and died this year. A declassified NSA statement, included in his 2014 workplace compensation claim, noted that “there is intelligence information from 2012 associating the hostile country to which Mr Beck travelled in the late 1990s with a high-powered microwave system weapon that may have the ability to weaken, intimidate or kill an enemy, over time, and without leaving evidence”. The unnamed “hostile country”, sources said, was Russia.

blocks.caption: Mike Beck, pictured in 2017, died this year after developing a rare form of Parkinson’s disease aged 45. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images

blocks.text: The first known AHIs among the contemporary batch of cases occurred in late 2014, when several US government employees at the consulate in Frankfurt, Germany, became ill. One was found unconscious in a consulate stairwell after feeling sudden, intense pressure on her chest and hearing a “high-pitched squeal”, Rey and Zill reported.

The next year, a researcher at a US defence institute – who asked the Guardian not to use her name – was on a tour of the Balkans, attending meetings with military officers from the host nations alongside US defence attaches. Her itinerary took in Montenegro, which was in the process of applying for Nato membership, and Serbia, a Russian ally that harboured resentments towards the US over the 1999 Nato bombing of Yugoslavia.

On her final evening in Belgrade, as she walked through lively pedestrianised streets to her hotel, the researcher was sure she spotted someone following her. Later, as she approached her hotel room, she felt “a sinking feeling, as though I was in a lift that was descending suddenly”, she recalled in a telephone interview.

Inside her room, she continued to feel odd sensations. “I just had this falling sensation, a feeling of gravity pulling at me, and nausea.” At one point, she turned on her government laptop and found the screen was flickering with blue static. The computer never worked again.

She said she was able to continue her trip, but in the subsequent weeks she felt weak, had difficulty speaking clearly and developed pain that felt “like a drill was going into my eye”. She was unable to focus at work. “I used up all my vacation, then my sick leave, then colleagues donated their leave. Eventually, I had to leave my job,” she said. It was only much later that she connected what had happened to her with reports about Havana syndrome.

blocks.caption: Marc Polymeropoulos has symptoms associated with Havana syndrome. Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The Guardian

blocks.text: The next cohort of AHI patients included people at the heart of a new CIA policy on Russia. In 2017, as Donald Trump took office for the first time, the agency launched a drive to push back against the increasingly brazen global reach of Moscow’s intelligence agencies.

“They wanted us to take the same kind of tactics and spirit we used in the global war on terror to the Russians,” said Marc Polymeropoulos, who was made deputy chief of operations for Europe and Eurasia in 2017. Polymeropoulos, who had spent most of his career in the Middle East, was one of several veterans of the “war on terror” who were moved to senior roles focused on Russia. Even as Trump publicly denied that Russia had interfered in the 2016 election, the agency made plans to push back hard against Russian activity.

“Obviously, we didn’t have permission to run lethal operations against the Russians, but we could do things we hadn’t done as much previously, such as enlist the help of multiple friendly services and expose the Russians for what they were doing,” said Polymeropoulos, in an interview at a restaurant just outside Washington.

In early December 2017, Polymeropoulos and another senior CIA executive made a liaison trip to Moscow, to meet their counterparts in Russia’s SVR and FSB intelligence services. The official meetings were ill-tempered and lacking in substance. Late one night, Polymeropoulos woke up suddenly in his hotel room. “I had vertigo and a splitting headache. I thought it was food poisoning at first, I thought I was going to puke and crap my brains out, and I remember being like, holy shit, the room is spinning and my ears are ringing,” he said.

On his return to Washington, Polymeropoulos struggled with a persistent migraine that would not subside, and with superiors who insisted his symptoms were unrelated to other AHIs. He saw a variety of doctors on his own time, but owing to the classified nature of his job he could not share details of where he had been when he became ill.

He left the CIA in 2019 and, frustrated at being stonewalled in his requests for medical assessment, became the first CIA officer to go public with a Havana syndrome story under their real name, telling the journalist Julia Ioffe about what happened in Moscow.

The resulting publicity prompted the CIA to send him to the Walter Reed military medical centre, where he was diagnosed with mild traumatic brain injury. In 2023 he was found eligible for compensation under the Havana Act, which authorised payments to “personnel who incur brain injuries from hostilities while on assignment”. The financial payout was modest, but he saw it as a moral victory after years of fighting for recognition.

blocks.caption: Marc Polymeropoulos struggled with a persistent migraine that would not subside. Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The Guardian

blocks.text: One early theory was that AHIs could be the result of data collection attempts gone wrong – a machine designed to pull classified data from operatives’ electronic devices that had unfortunate side-effects when turned up too high. That is still seen by some as a possibility, although even if intelligence collection was the initial idea, the damaging health effects would have quickly become apparent to the operators.

Some observers insisted the whole concept of “Havana syndrome” was an invention. They asked why, if Russia possessed a brain-frying weapon, it was not using it on a wider range of its enemies. Why were there not more reports of collateral victims?

The sociologist Robert Bartholomew and the neurologist Robert Baloh co-authored a book that declared the whole story a hoax – “a case study in the social construction of mass psychogenic illness” – borne of high-stress work environments and propagated by excitable journalists.

Douglas Fields, a cellular neuroscientist and author of several books about the brain, claimed in a journal article that the medical studies of patients which showed cognitive changes had used unsound methodology, and that theories of an energy weapon “defy the laws of physics”. Reports of Havana syndrome should be taken no more seriously than sightings of the Loch Ness monster, he suggested.

Other scientists, including some who had reviewed patients’ medical records, strongly disagreed. “The early scepticism was perfectly appropriate, but over time we started to see an increase in the number of individuals who have gone through clinical evaluations that cannot be faked,” said James Giordano, a professor emeritus of neurology at Georgetown University Medical Center and the forensic neuroscientist on the original cohort of cases from Havana.

“We are talking about objective signs that are presenting with a very distinct pattern,” Giordano said. Key symptoms included “a profound tumbling or falling sensation” as well as pressure in the head, chest and throat, and cognitive effects. It was true that chemical or drug exposure could cause similar symptoms, he said, but this would be visible on blood tests. Another key factor was the sudden onset and the sense of a specific location where the apparent attack felt strongest.

When the Biden administration took office in 2021, the then CIA director, Bill Burns, and the director of national intelligence, Avril Haines, vowed to get to the bottom of the issue. Burns met many of the AHI cohort, including Polymeropoulos, listening carefully to their stories and promising them a full investigation.

Burns also fired the CIA’s chief medical officer, who had infuriated some AHI patients by accusing them of faking their symptoms. The same year, more than 100 CIA operatives and other US government officials reported AHIs in locations around the world. In Vienna, there were so many hits that the work of the CIA station was essentially paralysed and the station chief recalled. A spate of government employees also reported incidents on US soil, including several who claimed to have been hit on the grounds of the White House. Was this an adversary stepping up its campaign, or was the increasing publicity about AHIs leading more people to misidentify other conditions or episodes as Havana syndrome?

Burns and Haines launched two investigations, one to re-examine intelligence on whether a foreign adversary was behind Havana syndrome, and another that convened a panel of scientists and physicians to determine whether it was even possible for a weapon to cause the symptoms.

blocks.caption: David Relman said there were dozens of cases ‘that were unusual in the distinctness of their features’. Photograph: Lea Suzuki/San Francisco Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images

blocks.text: Relman, a Stanford professor who chaired the scientific panel, said its members were given access to open source and classified scientific studies into pulsed radio frequency energy, which suggested that the science behind there being a “device” that could cause AHI symptoms was plausible. Scientists who disagreed were simply unaware of the research into such technology that had been taking place for decades in several countries, especially in the Soviet Union and then Russia, he said.

Regarding the medical results, Relman conceded that plenty – perhaps the vast majority – of AHI claims could be explained by other factors. But there were dozens of cases “that were unusual in the distinctness of their features and the near impossibility of explaining them based on known medical and environmental conditions”. In short: the publicity around AHIs may have prompted a wave of false reporting, but a core subset of cases seemed real.

Determining who may have carried out such attacks was beyond Relman’s purview. That fell to the second expert group, which in 2023 issued the assessment that it was “very unlikely” to be caused by a foreign adversary, dismaying many AHI patients who had hoped to finally receive closure on what caused their health problems.

Even people who have seen the intelligence on Havana syndrome can disagree on what it suggests. Two sources offered the Guardian radically different interpretations of what the classified data shows on possible Russian involvement.
One highlighted the lack of a “smoking gun”; a piece of human intelligence or an intercept that showed Russian operatives discussing a programme to use directed energy against Americans.

“Everyone has seen how strong our collection capabilities on Russia are,” the source said, referencing how US intelligence got hold of Putin’s war plans before his February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. “If this was really a large-scale Russian programme, we would have expected to see something in some of these channels, but we didn’t.”

Another former intelligence official disagreed: “If you’re waiting for an intercept of someone saying: ‘My name is Igor and I’m going to press the button on my secret laser’ before you have confidence, that’s probably never going to happen. But for any reasonable person who has access to the intelligence and knows how to read it, the Russian fingerprints are clear.”

If that is the case, it raises the question of why the 2023 intelligence community assessment found it “very unlikely” that a foreign actor was involved. At the end of the Biden administration, a tweaked version said that while five US intelligence agencies still found it “very unlikely”, one agency now believed there was a “roughly even chance” that a foreign actor had used “a novel weapon or prototype device” in a number of attacks.

This summer, both of those Biden-era assessments were rescinded by Trump’s director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, in a memo issued just before she left office. Gabbard said the earlier assessments were marred by “selective exclusion of evidence” and “mischaracterisation of sources”, though the statement did not release any new evidence or provide a revised assessment.

While Gabbard had a chequered reputation among the intelligence community, Mark Zaid, a lawyer who represents more than 30 AHI patients, welcomed her memo and said it was a first step to overturning a CIA cover-up. When asked why the CIA might have perpetrated such a cover-up, Zaid suggested it could be to protect its reputation after prior negligence. “This has built up to a level that the agency can’t let the truth get out because it’s going to reflect so poorly on them,” he said.

Burns, in a comment for Rey and Zill’s book, said it was “simply not true that there was a ‘cover-up’ by the CIA” and described the earlier investigation as “a rigorous effort across the entire intelligence community”.

Rey and Zill believe the purported cover-up was a result of multiple factors over many years. “There’s not a single cigar-filled backroom meeting that led to decisions getting made,” said Rey. “There was a lot of, ‘This is a pain in the ass’ or ‘The president’s not going to want to hear this’. There was bureaucratic dysfunction, careerism and things that just got in the way of proper investigation.”

One example he gave is the fact that the FBI sent criminal investigators, rather than counterintelligence investigators with access to classified information, to Havana after the attacks there. Another is a nascent investigation at CIA headquarters in late 2019 which reportedly found that, in some cases, phones linked to Russian intelligence operatives had been in the vicinity of suspected Havana syndrome incidents. These included the hits that year on the senior CIA officer in London and Warsaw.

blocks.caption: Rey and Zill believe the purported cover-up was a result of multiple factors over many years. Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The Guardian

blocks.text: In London, a suspicious phone had supposedly been just 10 metres (30ft) away from his hotel room. But when the then CIA director, Gina Haspel, was briefed on these findings, she allegedly complained it was not solid enough to take to the president, given how sensitive he was on Russia-related matters. “The meeting abruptly ended after Haspel shouted that if she took reports like this to President Trump, she would be fired as director,” Rey and Zill write.

Outside the CIA, some have uncovered intriguing leads about possible links between Russian operatives and AHIs. Christo Grozev, a journalist and investigator who has exposed several Russian intelligence operations, claimed leaked travel data suggested at least four potential crossovers between suspected AHIs and travel by officers from Unit 29155 of Russia’s GRU military intelligence, known for its campaign of sabotage and assassinations in western countries. He also said he had traced travel by “members of what appears to be a technical unit adjacent to 29155” to Cuba during the initial attacks.

Perhaps the most significant piece of evidence to emerge recently has been the alleged US government acquisition of a “Havana syndrome-style device” in an undercover operation. First reported by the independent journalist Sasha Ingber this year, two sources confirmed to the Guardian that a device had been acquired and brought to the US in late 2024 for testing, after a purchase from a dark-web seller.

Rey and Zill’s book recounts a meeting with a person who claimed to be part of the undercover team that acquired the device. The source told them the device was “man-portable”, shot non-thermal pulsed microwaves and was acquired from “a complex Russian illicit network”.

It was not believed to have been used in a Havana syndrome incident, but testing on animals has reportedly shown it may cause similar symptoms to AHIs, which could prove that building such a device is scientifically possible.

That would make the case for a weapon being involved in some incidents more plausible, and would also raise new and worrying questions. If such weapons have proliferated to the extent that one can be bought on the dark web, how many devices could be out there and who may have access to them? Could AHIs thus have not one perpetrator, but many? And is there a future in which such weapons become a widespread element of warfare? “We know the technology has reached a level that enables it to be used in weaponisable ways,” said Giordano. “I see that as a clear and present threat.”

For those who have had symptoms for years, the acquisition of the device and the rescinded intelligence assessments provide some hope that, one day, they will receive official confirmation that they were targeted by a foreign adversary. For many of them, the lack of recognition at home has angered them more than the attack itself.

“The Russians are our enemy, I put them in the same bucket as al-Qaida or the Taliban, or any other groups I worked against,” said Polymeropoulos. “Do I want to see them held accountable? Of course. But I’m actually more upset and feel more of a betrayal from my own government.”

items: The Havana Syndrome by Michael Rey and Oriana Zill de Granados is published by Crown Publishing in the US on 13 October and by WH Allen in the UK on 15 October.

articles.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
articles.summary: After four years, a Ukrainian man is set to stand trial in Hamburg accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream pipelines.

blocks.text: Image source, Swedish Coast Guard
Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022
BySarah Rainsford
Eastern and Southern Europe correspondent
Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.

Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.
But German police were already closing in on him.

After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.

Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".
Both he and his country have denied any involvement.
Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor
It was 02:03 am on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.

There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.
Both have been inoperable ever since.
Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.
They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.
Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.
As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.
Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.
But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.
They went on following the forensic crumbs.
Eventually they led to Ukraine.

blocks.caption: A map showing Nord Stream pipelines running through Europe

blocks.text: The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.
In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.
That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.

He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.
But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.

Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.

By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.
Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.
The saboteurs
None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.
But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them.
"Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."
Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.
That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.
Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution.
"Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.
The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution.
Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence.
"At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained.
Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia

blocks.text: Image source, Omar Marques/Getty Images
Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia
Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far.
Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.
He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation.
Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him.
Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning.
He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver.
But he is a civilian.
Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.
In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war".
As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more."
Croatia is a different matter.
Political ripples
The implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg.

After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.
It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv.
It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone.
When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that".
This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further.
"I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully.
He argued that the Nord Stream pipelines had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed that to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe.
"Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did."
First in the dock
Serhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial.
Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated.
Those who know Serhii K call him a patriot.
He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023.
His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing.
They are not saying, though.
And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either.
His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up.
I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot.
More on the Nord Stream blasts

articles.title: Flydubai attacker began a 'drift towards extremism and terrorism' in Australia, UAE says
articles.summary: The United Arab Emirates' attorney-general also alleges the co-pilot was trying to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's airport.

blocks.text: According to Shamsi, interrogations of the 29-year-old pilot revealed he had been inspired by al-Qaeda's 11 September attacks in the US in 2001.

"The findings indicated that signs of his drift towards extremism and terrorism first emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia," the attorney-general was quoted as saying by the UAE's state news agency Wam on Friday.
"During that period, he was influenced by takfiri [radical] ideology through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks."

The Wam report also said the pilot had told investigators "he had prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach".
"He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim," Wam said.
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported the man was issued an Australian student visa in 2014 and studied in the country in 2015-17, before leaving.

This week, the Sydney Morning Herald unearthed tweets from al-Mammami's now-deleted X account in which he referred to his five years spent studying abroad in Australia, Britain, and New Zealand, as "the golden years of my religious commitment".
More than 170 passengers and crew were on board flight FZ1073 on 30 September.
In the days after the incident, Australian authorities confirmed they were looking into the man's links to Australia.

The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team - made up of the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Victoria Police and the country's security agency ASIO - said it was "investigating the man's links to Australia".

articles.title: US country music star Ella Langley cancels show due to 'security threat'
articles.summary: Police say they checked the concert venue in Tulsa, Oklahoma but "could not find any threat".

blocks.text: US country music star Ella Langley has said she had to cancel her sold-out concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma on Friday night, due to a "serious security threat".
The singer made what she called the "incredibly difficult" decision around two hours before the show at the 19,000-seater arena was due to start.
In a post on Instagram, the 27-year-old said the threat involved "the safety of my fans, the venue staff and my team".
Cpt Richard Meulenberg from Tulsa Police Department said a person had called saying "great harm" would be done at the event with "shots fired and bombs."
He stated his team had checked the venue at BOK Center several times before the show and "could not find any threat".
"The event was ready to go," he added, saying officers with sniffer dogs did a sweep of the arena again after the phone call was made.
"We could not find a credible threat," he said, stressing that the person who had made the call "disrupted this entire event" for thousands of Langley fans.
The star - who did not give any further details - also apologised to her fans, saying additional information regarding ticket refunds "will be shared as soon as possible".

BOK Center issued its own statement, saying that "the safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed.
"We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologise to fans who planned to attend."
In September, Langley's country smash Choosin' Texas overtook Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You to become the longest-running number one single in US chart history.
Its success helped the singer from Alabama to sweep the Academy of Country Music Awards in May.

articles.title: Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
articles.summary: Fresh details reveal how the 40-year-old businessman flew and crossed regional borders while seriously ill.

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Nearly 70 potential contacts have been placed under quarantine in Nairobi
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.

The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.

That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.

Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo

The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.

blocks.caption: A map showing the man's journey from DR Congo through Uganda to Kenya

blocks.text: The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.

Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.

The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The man's funeral was held under strict safety protocols

blocks.text: The man's funeral was held under strict safety protocols
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.

Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya

Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.

The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.

The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.
BBC Africa podcasts

articles.title: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
articles.summary: Students taking to the streets in France have become a focal point in the country's increasingly polarised politics.

blocks.text: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
Image source, Getty Images
Hundreds of thousands of students have protested across France since the end of last month
ByNick Beake
Europe correspondent
As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets.
"There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school.
"We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen."

He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.
Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down.
"They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population."

The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Massicella, second left, and her friends have been protesting in Lille

blocks.text: Massicella, second left, and her friends have been protesting in Lille
The protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country.

Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter.
The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system.
Watch: Marseille school students explain why they're protesting

The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them.
On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million.
But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them.
Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem.
It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages.
When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils).
"It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Teachers, including Marine Monins and Marjorie Roussel, have joined their students in calling for change

blocks.text: Teachers, including Marine Monins and Marjorie Roussel, have joined their students in calling for change
On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget.
But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country.
"It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest.
"It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Police have been accused of heavy-handed tactics

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Police have been accused of heavy-handed tactics
The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries.
So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry.
More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks.

But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers.
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens.

Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade.
A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth.

"For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether."
Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kaspar says strangers have been hijacking some protests

blocks.text: Kaspar says strangers have been hijacking some protests

But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests.
"These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world."
Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard.

Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring.

"Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Marine Le Pen has condemned damage to schools

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Marine Le Pen has condemned damage to schools
The protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise.
More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country.
But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape.
The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant.
Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration.
Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race.
Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jean-Luc Mélenchon has been supportive of the demonstrations

blocks.text: Jean-Luc Mélenchon has been supportive of the demonstrations
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks.
Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth.

He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history.
Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are looking to the past for inspiration.
"I personally want to reproduce 1968!" Massicella declares in Lille, as she nears the end of the protest march.
Le Pen has stayed away from the protests and her most notable interventions have come in condemning the damage to schools, which is said to run into the millions of euros.
She has also suggested that parents of children who have committed the vandalism should pay for repairs.
The principle of casseur-payeur – those who break have to pay – has been an impassioned topic that has dominated French media this week.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The 1968 protests have carved an indelible memory in French social history

blocks.text: The 1968 protests have carved an indelible memory in French social history
The problem for President Macron is that there is no quick fix.

This is not a scenario where there is an unpopular piece of legislation that can be withdrawn in a hasty reverse ferret the prime minister is tasked with performing. That was the case with the gilets jaunes – the relentless protest in high vis jackets over a fuel tax rise nearly a decade ago.
Wholesale reform of the education system would cost billions – in new classrooms, new facilities, new teachers – and take years to achieve.
And changes that may seem more easily done – such as a reduction of the length of the school day – would be hugely problematic to implement logistically.
What is more, any proposals which appease the students and end the current protests would have to be agreed at a time when France's finances are in a mess.

The cost of servicing the national debt each year has now exceeded the core state education budget. Under the 2027 draft budget, there will be a 1.7% rise in education spending - but this is an under-inflation increase.
Le Pen has vowed to cut public spending even further if she enters the Élysée Palace.
She is banking that her promises to cut debt, curb migration and restrict certain benefits to French citizens will eclipse any criticism over her position on the protesting pupils.
For her, discipline, a traditional curriculum and pride in France's history should be the defining features of every classroom.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Many students have said they will not back down from protesting
