blocks.text: Many students have said they will not back down from protesting
But many students are showing little sign of backing down from another French tradition.
"In France, we have this tradition and history of revolting," says Alcidor in Paris.
"That's the way we gained our rights and the way we will always gain them. That's our spirit."
As the rain came outside the Lycée Voltaire central in Paris this week, the reality of having been up early once again to block the main gate started to kick in and the energy of the crowd dipped.
But not for long.
A huge cheer erupted as a senior teacher unlocked the hulking front door and poked her head out into the street.
"The canteen is still open."
The hunger for better schools among France's youth and better days for everyone else will not be so easily sated.
Additional reporting by Bruno Boelpaep and Manon Prat

articles.title: Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
articles.summary: The US president hopes to ease his party's pain before next month's midterm elections, writes the BBC's North America correspondent.

blocks.text: Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.
Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.
Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.
The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.
As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.
For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.
He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.
His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear.
It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy".
"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.
It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.
The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.
Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.
Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.
With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.

But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.

Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

articles.title: Three men found guilty of murdering Australian brothers and US friend in Mexico
articles.summary: Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend Carter Rhoad were on a surf trip when they were killed in an apparent botched robbery.

blocks.text: Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024.

The men's full names could not be given for legal reasons, and they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús. They are yet to be sentenced - but are likely to spend the rest of their lives in a prison.
Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them".
During the trial in the northern Baja California state, the court heard that the tourists were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck in a secluded beach area.
Their bodies were later found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads.
The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the coastal area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico.
Debra Robinson and her husband Martin have been at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial, and delivered emotional testimony during closing arguments before Friday's verdict.
"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin said.
Family members of Carter Rhoad joined the trial by video link.

Speaking to media outside court a week ago, Debra Robinson said the couple were "deeply grateful" to Australians for the outpouring of support they had received and that they "feel the love and their arms around us".
During the month-long trial, the prosecution had sought 150 years in prison for each of the three defendants.

In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo alias "El Kekas", was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.
At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.
The beach town has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.
The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.
Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week when their families were able to identify them.
At the time, the surfer community in Ensenada turned out in force to honour the men by paddling out at a popular surfing spot and throwing flowers into the sea.

Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.
Amid the demands for action, state Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila tried to ease public fears about the widespread violence.
"Baja California is and will continue to be a state with safe tourism for the thousands of people who visit us from the rest of the country and the world", she said.
"I send my condolences and solidarity to the families at this difficult time."

articles.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
articles.summary:
Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers

A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some…

blocks.text: A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.
It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.
Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.
Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.
The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.
The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.

The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.

In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.

Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.
According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.

The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.

“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.

Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.

The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.

Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.

This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”

When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.

Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

articles.title: Three men found guilty of murders of Australian surfer brothers and US friend in Mexico
articles.summary:
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, 30 and 33, and friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were killed on a surfing trip in 2024

  • Get our

blocks.text: A Mexican judge has convicted three men of the 2024 murders of two Australian surfers and their American friend in a case that sparked international outrage.

Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in a suspected robbery.
The deaths of the trio sparked an outpouring of grief and condemnation in Australia and the United States.

Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. He and two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were found guilty on Friday local time.
Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, traveled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.
“They took our sons from our lives forever,” said Debra Robinson, who testified on the final day of the trial. “What hurts us most is that, in their final hours, they were treated with such cruelty.”
Addressing the court at the start of the trial, Martin Robinson described his sons’ murders as “hell”.
“It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons,” he said.
Rhoad’s mother, Page, and his fiance, Natalie Weirtz, also participated in the hearing in a video call from the United States.
“The accused are guilty and must be punished so that no other family suffers the same pain,” Weirtz said. “Since Carter’s death, I feel paranoid and isolated.”
The surfers were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found in a clifftop shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads.

Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while traveling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.
More details soon …

articles.title: Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Israeli airport, UAE prosecutors say
articles.summary:
Hammam al-Hammami is believed to have been targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv

The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a passenger jet flying from Dubai…

blocks.text: The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a passenger jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week was planning to launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Israel’s international airport, prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said on Friday.

Hammam al-Hammami attacked the plane’s Indian pilot with an emergency axe, but failed to prevent his badly injured colleague from opening the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower his assailant.
Passengers then tried to control the aircraft, which was safely landed in Saudi Arabia by an off-duty relief pilot who was among about 180 passengers.

Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney-general of the UAE, said on Friday that al-Hammami, who is in Emirate custody, had admitted he had tried to execute a “premeditated terrorist plot to … launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv, with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”.

The 29-year-old, who was hired by flydubai, a government-owned low-cost airline, began a process of radicalisation while studying in Australia when he was influenced by the hardline takfiri ideology through reading extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks, al-Shamsi said in a statement.

“[Al-Hammami] subsequently developed … ideas advocating violence and terrorism. He also drew inspiration from the 11 September 2001 attacks, and the idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking. According to his confession, this was linked to his decision to pursue a career in aviation.”

Over the weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. He left the country without completing his engineering degree.
New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation after police confirmed al-Hammami underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.

There has been widespread concern about how al-Hammami was able to pass vetting and join a crew flying to Israel. An Omani national, he earned a distance-learning aviation management degree from Buckinghamshire New University in 2023 and was employed by Oman Air from 2020-24, joined Royal Air Maroc in early 2025 and worked there for several months before moving to flydubai in January 2026.

Security officials have been keen to understand if al-Hammami was acting alone or had become involved with a group such as al-Qaida or Islamic State, which could suggest further such attacks might be planned. Emirate authorities believe this is not the case.

“In the presence of his lawyer and with all legally prescribed safeguards ensured, the suspect provided a detailed confession outlining his motives and the stages of planning and execution. He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim,” al-Shamsi said.
Investigators have found al-Hammami had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the flight route ‌and the airport”, the Emirati state news agency WAM reported.
The passengers on board the aircraft were overwhelmingly Israeli, with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailing them and the pilot for their bravery after the foiled attack.

articles.title: BBC breaks down video of the aftermath of New York City ICE shooting
articles.summary: The BBC's Nada Tawfik goes through new dramatic body cam footage that shows the tense moments when police arrive on scene.

blocks.text: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement shot and wounded a man in his car in New York City on Thursday while his five-year-old son was in the back seat. Body cam footage released by the New York Police Department on Friday, shows its officers arriving on scene and helping the man. The BBC’s Nada Tawfik breaks down the newly released footage of the aftermath of the shooting.

articles.title: Schools crisis in France: Investment fails to inspire confidence
articles.summary: For weeks, schoolchildren in France have been protesting the failing education system. Compared to many other countries, France invests heavily in education but critics say that the funds are not…

image.caption: University students have joined in on the protests to support schoolchildrenImage: Christophe Agostinis/MAXPPP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Rats in the toilets, leaking roofs, broken heating systems: Cellphone videos filmed by French schoolchildren and circulating on social media bear witness to the dilapidated infrastructure in many educational institutions across France.

At the Lycee Paul Eluard in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, a center of the current protests, young people have reported that there are vermin in the building, and say burst pipes are a regular occurrence. In nearby Pantin, pupils complained that windows couldn't be opened, even when temperatures soared to 40 degrees Celsius (over 104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer.
Pupils also complain of overcrowded classrooms and frequently cancelled lessons.
The protests, which have erupted all over the country, show no sign of coming to an end.
France students demand better schools
Problems of centralization

Yet, by EU standards, France invests a substantial amount in its education system — 6.7% of its GDP. The fact that this investment has not translated into a better learning environment may be partly attributable to the way responsibilities are divided.

The central government in Paris mainly deals with paying teachers, and setting national curricula. But the responsibility for maintaining school buildings lies with France's various levels of local government. For elementary schools, the administration responsible is the municipality; for "colleges" (lower secondary schools, ages 11–15) it is the wider department, and for lycees (upper secondary schools, ages 15–18) it is the region.

Depending on the region, the local authorities have different financial possibilities at their disposal, and must plan renovation projects themselves. Progress on making improvements is often very slow as a result. In addition, more than two-thirds of their budget is already allocated to staffing costs and pension payments, leaving relatively little room for investment.
Dilapidated infrastructure

Over 80% of elementary school buildings in France are more than 50 years old. An estimated 10 to 20% of all school buildings are considered to be in serious need of renovation. In many instances, politicians have been trying to address the problem. Ile-de-France, which covers Paris and the region surrounding it, approved a 10-year program of renovation and expansion for the period 2017 to 2027 at a cost of €6.6 billion ($7.4 billion).

According to the local authorities, two-thirds of upper secondary pupils now attend a new school, or one that has been renovated. But even after mold has been removed and roofs repaired, it is still rare for buildings to have effective protection against the summer heat. It is also a bitter irony that some buildings newly constructed at considerable expense, or renovated just a few years earlier, have been damaged in the recent protests.
France students protest school conditions
Macron tried in vain to address problem

Imbalances are also evident in ongoing education expenditure. While France invests a comparatively large amount in upper secondary education, according to OECD calculations Paris spends less per primary school pupil than the average for industrialized countries. Education researchers emphasize that it is precisely these early years that lay the foundation for subsequent academic success.

The governments put in place by French President Emmanuel Macron have attempted to address this imbalance. Since 2017, class sizes in the first years of primary school have been halved in socially disadvantaged areas, and around 16,000 additional teaching posts created.

Amid the ongoing protests, the government has said it now intends to recruit more than 3,000 supply teachers at short notice. French Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced that software would be used to identify schools that are in a particularly difficult situation.

These announcements are the government's first concrete response to the demands of the students, who have been demonstrating for almost two weeks now, calling for better facilities in secondary schools, more supply teachers and greater investment in the education system generally.

blocks.caption: Schoolchildren and students all over France have joined in on the protestsImage: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

blocks.text: Increasing deficiencies

The latest scores for the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s (OECD) program for international student assessment (Pisa), which were published in September, illustrate the scale of the problems in the education system. According to the results, more than one in three 15-year-olds in France no longer achieve a basic level of competence in mathematics, for example.

Macron's reform of the upper secondary education system has also been criticized. The abolition of academic streaming in favor of specialist subjects selected by the individual was meant to give pupils greater freedom of choice. However, the large number of possible subject combinations make it difficult to timetable lessons. Students complain that they have too many free periods and longer school days.

The problems also extend to universities. A lecturer at a Paris university described a seminar attended by 50 students — so many that they have to fetch chairs from other rooms or sit on the floor. So far, she said, the university administration had done nothing about it.

blocks.caption: Pupils and students in Bron, a suburb of Lyon, called for better learning conditions and investment in the education systemImage: Pittore/NEIRDAPROD/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cancelled lessons

Compared with pupils in other EU countries, French schoolchildren have a high number of teaching hours per school year — on paper, at least. But the French Court of Accounts recorded that 9% of lessons at state colleges were cancelled in the 2023–24 school year. A study from the school year 2024–25 suggests that only around 12% of lessons cancelled at short notice are covered by other teachers.

The relatively low salaries of French teachers compared to those in neighboring countries are also a problem. OECD data shows that after 15 years in the profession teachers at lower secondary schools in France only earn about half as much as their German counterparts.
Broken promises of equality

France takes pride in its republican model of education, which is supposed to provide all children with equal opportunities, irrespective of their background. In reality, academic success in France is much more dependent on parents' socioeconomic circumstances than in many other countries. This is also apparent in that children from poorer families are far more likely to be affected by the cancellation of lessons.

The government's financial room for maneuver is currently restricted by the country's precarious budgetary situation. Although the draft budget for 2027 includes an additional €1.2 billion for the Ministry of Education, there are also plans to cut teaching posts, on the grounds that pupil numbers are falling.

blocks.caption: Students also protested against the media coverage of the problems in the education systemImage: Raphael Lafargue/abaca/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protests in the run-up to the presidential election

It's not just videos of dilapidated school buildings that are circulating on social media. As the discontent has spread, there is also footage of demonstrations where people carry placards with political slogans that have little to do with education policy. Some videos show burning barricades and clashes with the police, which faces accusations of usingdisproportionate force.

blocks.caption: Saint-Denis mayor, Bally Bagayoko, tried to shield student protesters from riot police Image: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP

blocks.text: Some members of the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party have associated themselves with the protesting students. Lawmakers have appeared at school blockades and shared related videos. The government has accused LFI of deliberately exploiting young people's anger for political purposes, an allegation that the party rejects.
With the French presidential election just six months away, the protests over the crisis in education are evolving into a power struggle.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Thai Queen makes first solo flight in fighter jet
articles.summary: Thailand’s Queen Suthida made her first solo flight in a fighter jet, according to the Thai Royal Household.

blocks.text: Thailand's Queen Suthida made her first solo flight in a fighter jet, according to the Thai Royal Household.
The Queen was shown boarding a Gripen on 8 October at an airfield in Surat Thani province, southern Thailand, while King Maha Vajiralongkorn watched from the ground.
The Royal Household has said she is an experienced pilot, having logged about 1,188 hours across several types of aircraft since she began flying in 2010.
She also co-piloted aircraft carrying the King on official visits to other countries, the Royal Household said.

articles.title: JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he will not watch it
articles.summary: The planned execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad would be the first military execution in more than 60 years.

blocks.text: The Pentagon announced earlier this week it would execute Hasan by firing squad, the first of its kind since the end of World War Two. Then on Thursday US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be livestreamed for the public.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," said Hegseth.
The BBC has asked the White House whether Trump supported the plans.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Vance said: "I see these announcements. I don't know that that's actually going to happen."
The vice-president said that Hasan was meant to treat soldiers for mental illness and other problems and "took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived".
The announcement over the livestream plans has been met with criticism from both political parties.

Republican Senator John Curtis pointed to Rome's history of a "bloody spectacle" corrupting people who watched them, warning that public executions erode civilisations "when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment".
Curtis said that Hegseth's plan "risks feeding that appetite" and urged him to reconsider.
"The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent," he said.
Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN that the idea was "disgusting" and reminiscent of executions carried out by the Islamic State group.
The US Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the decision to publicly livestream Hasan's execution, expressing "shock and great sorrow" in a statement.
The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming it would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture".

articles.title: This loaf of rye bread is selling for $60 in New York. Is it worth it?
articles.summary: Rye opened in Manhattan last month, offering a titular loaf made from water, imported rye flour and salt. The fourth ingredient, according to the bakery, is time. But while some people have said the…

image.caption: The bread sold at Rye in Manhattan is made from water, imported rye flour and salt. The fourth ingredient, according to the bakery, is time. (Submitted by Elazar Sontag)

blocks.text: The Current

Rye opened in Manhattan last month, offering a titular loaf made from water, imported rye flour and salt. The fourth ingredient, according to the bakery, is time. But while some people have said the price tag is exorbitant, others seem happy to pay.
Online commenters decry high price for single loaf, but others seem happy to pay
LISTEN | 'There were people who were coming in and buying 10 loaves':
The Current7:56Would you buy a $60 loaf of bread?
A bakery in New York is selling a loaf of rye bread for $60 US ($85 Cdn). But while many have criticized the price as exorbitant, a food critic who tried it says it tells a more complex story.
“Is the bread delicious? The answer is yes. Is the bread worth it? [That] I think is a much more complicated question,” said Elazar Sontag, a food critic for the Washington Post.

Austrian baker Martin Auer opened Rye in Manhattan last month, making the titular loaf from water, imported rye flour and salt. The fourth ingredient, according to the bakery, is time: 24 hours for the dough to rest, ferment and develop, then 70 minutes in the oven. The loaf weighs about 1.5 kilograms, and is also sold in smaller portions.

Auer’s family have been in the bread business since 1936, and offer the same loaf in Vienna for a fraction of the price, just over €14 ($22 Cdn). The New York loaf’s price tag caught the attention of many on social media, with one TikToker describing Auer as either “a criminal or an evil genius” for capitalizing on New York’s taste for hype.

The Current contacted Rye with questions, but did not receive a response. The bakery previously told Sontag that the New York pricing reflects rent, wages and transportation, as well as costs related to development, design, packaging and the work of making the bread itself.
Sontag tried the loaf and wrote about it in the Washington Post. He spoke to The Current’s Matt Galloway about what he thought. Here is part of their conversation.
I'm really glad to have you here, in part because you have had the bread. What is it like?

I can confirm the tab, it is very expensive. Even knowing exactly what I was going for, when I saw that number come up on the little screen before I tapped my phone, it is kind of an eyebrow-raising moment.

The bread itself is delicious … people aren't really talking about the taste of the bread because to most people it's kind of beside the point. But if what you really are wondering is, is the bread delicious? The answer is yes. Is the bread worth it? [That] I think is a much more complicated question.
Part of it is the experience of going to the bakery, right? You said it's like an Apple store in some ways?
It has this very stern, but also sort of aspirational feel that I think will be familiar to anyone who shops at designer clothing stores … [or] people who buy their technology from Apple.

Apple similarly is sort of going for a certain kind of aspirational living, very clean, very minimal. It's not necessarily what you expect from a bakery. There's so many kinds of signifiers in there about lifestyle, right? You feel like you're walking into a place that's telling you how you should want to live, as opposed to necessarily just selling you a loaf of bread.
Persistent high food costs felt by shoppers
Who is buying a $60 loaf of bread?
Well, the short answer is, at the moment, a lot of people, because of this discourse and how far it has travelled.

But I actually asked one of the employees … and he said that a lot of people were coming just because they were curious. But he also said that it should be noted it's in a very wealthy New York neighbourhood. And that there were people who were coming in and buying 10 loaves. Now, that's about $600 of bread.
The owner has admitted that the same loaf sells for much less in Austria. You heard one of those people from social media at the beginning. Is this person a criminal or an evil genius?
I mean, probably neither. I think really this person is sort of just fitting into the long and storied tradition of kind of outlandish New York businesses.

I think the idea that people have latched onto — that this is really a sign of some new awful era of New York and a time when Americans can just sort of be hoodwinked and cheated — there's something there. I think the way that social media amplifies these sorts of conversations can make our culture feel very, very bleak.
Rye bakery in New York. Food critic Elazar Sontag says the store has a 'very stern but also sort of aspirational feel.' (Submitted by Elazar Sontag)

But, you know, as I pointed out in my column when I was writing about the bread, New York is a city of ridiculous contradictions. The idea that a $60 loaf of bread is so novel in a city where you could get a sushi dinner for one that costs a thousand? It's a little silly to me. Of course, the bread is also totally ridiculous, but I don't know that it's an indicator of some evil genius. It's certainly not criminal, as long as people are willing to sign up for the bread. What's he doing wrong? I mean, it's a little outlandish, but how outlandish is it for New York?

Bloomberg called this a K-shaped loaf of bread, pointing to the idea of the K-shape economy, which has this huge gap between the rich and the poor. What do you make of that? The bread is stamped, so if you buy the loaf of bread, everybody knows that it's not just a normal loaf of bread — this is the $60 loaf. Is this just about conspicuous consumption?
The shortest, shortest answer is probably yes. But it's not about the loaf of bread and I think people understand … that the loaf of bread is a symbol, right.

People are getting on the internet and saying, I think one of the most common lines right now is: bread is supposed to be a food of the working class, and the poor. It's flour and water — and how are we making something that is about access and about nourishment a symbol of this just sort of disgusting, offensive level of wealth. I take that, but I think it's important to remember that this is not a bakery that dropped into a working-class, under-resourced neighbourhood, and now suddenly the only option people have is this $60 bread.

items: A Manitoba farmer had a surplus of potatoes. So he gave millions of them away
How the humble cabbage got this P.E.I. woman a shout out in the New York Times
Behold the pawpaw, the tropical-tasting ‘alien banana’ that grows right here in Canada

blocks.text: I think that the tension and the anxiety is that it does point to something very real in America, certainly very real in New York, about this K-shaped economy. It's ostentatious, it comes in this bag that's printed with big blocky RYE letters. And you know, it does feel like a status symbol, and I think it does say something a little foreboding about our culture right now, that bread is a status symbol. But avocado toast was a status symbol 10 or 15 years ago.
What do you do with a $60 loaf of bread? Do you make avocado toast with it? Is it a sandwich? Do you just dip it in olive oil?
You savour it … you eat it very slowly.
Audio produced by Amanda Grant. Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.

articles.title: Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
articles.summary: Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the tech firm admits customers may experience disruption to digital services due to the attacks.

blocks.text: Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.
Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.

Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.
Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".
Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".
Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.
It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".
The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.

The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.
Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.
Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.
Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".
Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".

Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.
Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.
Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.

But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

articles.title: Man named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
articles.summary: The left-wing candidate won a narrow victory in a remote district in the Peruvian Andes, exit polls show.

blocks.text: A man named Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has secured a narrow victory in Peru's local elections, exit polls show.
The candidate for the centre-left Ahora Nación party was elected mayor of Queropalca, a remote district in the Peruvian Andes.
Some 229 residents voted for the 45-year-old, putting him ahead of the second-place candidate from right-wing Renovación Popular Perú by just 25 votes.
Despite being elected to represent fewer than 1,000 people, his forenames being those of two notorious fascist dictators has drawn outsized international attention to the small corner of the country.
Data from Peru's elections office showed a little over 700 people had participated in the election, with Simeon securing around 34% of the vote.
He was born in the district in the central department of Huánuco, some 360km (224 miles) from the capital, Lima, according to his candidate profile.

That he shares his name with Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini - "two of the most well-known figures of 20th-Century European totalitarian regimes" - has made his candidacy a "striking event", local outlet Peru21 reported.
Despite the curiosity generated by his name, local media noted that Hitler Guesclin Alba Sánchez had been elected mayor of Yúngar in 2018.
He reportedly beat rival candidate Lenin Vladimir Rodríguez Valverde after campaigning on the slogan "I'm the good Hitler".

A politician named Adolf Hitler Uunona attracted similar attention in 2020 after winning local elections in Namibia - a former German colony where Adolf and other Germanic first names are not uncommon.

articles.title: Macron and Steinmeier struggle to revive Franco-German ties
articles.summary: Presidents Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Emmanuel Macron are about to step down from their offices. Their meeting in France made it clear how urgently the Franco-German partnership needs new momentum.

image.caption: Presidents Steinmeier (l) and Macron and their wives met in Paris for a farewellImage: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The German delegation passed through Paris without being hindered by the student strikes taking place on the streets of Paris. The motorcades moved through the French capital without disruption. Around the Arc de Triomphe and the Champs-Elysees, however, traffic was at a standstill for hours. Due to the high-profile visit, the streets were cordoned off over a wide area.

Emmanuel Macron had decided on a special gesture to send off Frank-Walter Steinmeier, his German guest: The military honors took place under the Arc de Triomphe. And so, early in the morning, the German national anthem rang out in the heart of Paris — amid sunshine and bitter cold.

It was a generous gesture of friendship and symbolism, yet it seemed to be from a bygone era. In both countries, populists on the political fringes are gaining support. In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) ranks first in nationwide polls. In France, Emmanuel Macron could soon be succeeded by either Jean-Luc Melenchon of the far left or Marine Le Pen of the far right.

Added to this is an economic crisis that threatens prosperity. Unresolved issues of social justice are driving younger generations into the streets. At the same time, social media is increasingly becoming a tool of disinformation and "accelerating doubts about democracy," Macron said in Paris.

While the AfD may soon form its first state government in Saxony-Anhalt, President Steinmeier remained confident. He insisted that Germany would continue to "play a leading role in Europe" in the future and that Germans would remain good Europeans. But he did not say where he drew this certainty from. Questions from journalists were not permitted at the joint press conference at the Elysee Palace.
A future, but no plan

Political scientist Jacob Ross isn't surprised by this. Both Macron and Steinmeier lack a "genuine agenda for Germany, France, and Europe." Both represent political systems that "seek to respond to 21st-century crises with 20th-century solutions," said the expert on German-French relations at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP).

Even though Steinmeier and Macron have different political styles, Ross sees parallels — especially where their policies have failed. One example of this is strategic foreign policy issues, such as dealing with Russia. "For a long time, they pursued a policy based on integrating Russia into Europe, and then both were overwhelmed by the events of 2022 and had to adjust their course," said Ross. Since then, both have merely reacted to current affairs, according to the political scientist.
Little support for Macron's ideas
Emmanuel Macron has made some bold moves for Europe, but without support from Berlin, says Ross. Germany's political leadership has long reacted with caution to proposals from Paris.

A joint initiative that both countries recently promoted to the European Commission is aimed at combating unfair competition. Countries that gain an advantage through unfair practices should face strict European measures.

Macron joined German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in speaking out in favor of this. Although China was not explicitly named, the initiative is seen to be primarily aimed at that country. Beijing uses enormous subsidies to support its companies, whose products flood the European market, while European firms continue to face barriers when trying to access the Chinese market.
How Europe's defense sector is trying to gear up

Germany and France have also long sought greater cooperation in the defense sector. Yet major joint defense projects are making little progress. When the planned joint fighter jet, the FCAS, fell through in June, officials emphasized ongoing cooperation on the future MGCS main battle tank. And yet differences on this became apparent during the state visit.

As German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius arrived in Paris, French Chief of the General Staff Fabien Mandon stated during a hearing in the French National Assembly that Germany had decided to withdraw from the tank project. A day later, Mandon clarified that he had expressed himself ambiguously. But some observers believe that such misunderstandings are a sign of dissatisfaction on both sides — below the political level — regarding cooperation with the other partner.

It is this political level that often ends up having to set the record straight in such cases. This time was no exception: Pistorius firmly refuted the claim that the project was on the verge of being scrapped. "The MGCS project is not over; it is not dead; it has not been terminated by anyone — quite the contrary. It is a core project of Franco-German cooperation on land systems," said the German defense minister.

The focus is primarily on digital information processing in combat, as well as unmanned and automated systems. Germany and France would continue their cooperation, Pistorius insisted, and MGCS is an important future project for both countries and their armed forces.

blocks.caption: The French and German Presidents took part in a ceremony in the heart of ParisImage: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The future of defense and space

On Friday, the presidents of France and Germany visited several facilities near Bordeaux that are closely linked to space exploration and nuclear deterrence. These include ArianeGroup, a Franco-German company that, among other things, manufactures the nuclear-capable M51 missiles for French nuclear submarines. The itinerary also included visits to startups that are looking far into the future.

It was unofficially reported during the visit that this focus of the trip was a personal priority for Macron. The French president has long spoken of a European dimension to France's nuclear deterrent. Considering announcements from the US saying it would reduce its commitment to Europe, his views are gaining increasing traction.

As early as 2020, Macron proposed a strategic dialogue on the role of French nuclear weapons in European security. Several countries, including Germany, have since expressed interest. Now, further steps are being considered. The focus is on what Macron once called "forward deterrence," such as joint military exercises and visits to strategically important locations. A permanent deployment of French nuclear weapons in other countries remains off the table. Furthermore, according to French nuclear doctrine, France always retains sole decision-making authority over the use of its nuclear weapons.

Steinmeier's two-day state visit to France ended on Friday afternoon. So far, there has been little sign of new momentum in Franco-German relations. This makes it all the more urgent for the successors to the two presidents to develop a shared vision for the future of the relationship between the two countries starting next year.

Macron and Steinmeier will step down from their posts almost simultaneously in 2027 after ten years in office. The state visit to France thus also served as a final joint meeting, marked by some ceremonial farewells.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Author or artificial intelligence? Literature in crisis
articles.summary: AI is a hot topic at this year's Frankfurt Book Fair. An international literary scandal raises questions about machine-generated texts.

image.caption: The pavilion of the Guest of Honor, the Czech Republic, at the 2026 Frankfurt Book FairImage: Hannes P. Albert/AFP

blocks.text: It's the hot-button topic at the Frankfurt Book Fair: How profoundly will artificial intelligence transform the book industry, and how can this transformation be regulated?

Given the warnings about the technology's long-term risks to humanity as a whole, such debates might seem rather narrow in scope. In reality, however, they concern very concrete issues — copyright protection, the power of major tech corporations and the future of creative work. Many of those involved agree that the political measures taken don't go far enough.
This year, however, another aspect has entered the debate: Can we actually recognize when a text has been written with the help of artificial intelligence, and how can it be proven?

These are the questions being asked in the current literary scandal surrounding Haitian-Canadian author Thélyson Orélien. His debut novel, "C'était ça ou mourir," (It Was Either That or Die) was published in Canada in the spring and then in France in late summer.

blocks.caption: The controversy around Thélyson Orélien's book has sparked a larger debate on AI and authorshipImage: Joel Saget/AFP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The migration story was universally acclaimed, with translation rights sold in more than 20 languages. The book even made the longlist for the prestigious Prix Goncourt.

Then, suddenly, allegations emerged that the book had been written almost entirely using AI. Orélien, until then a rising literary star, suddenly found himself branded a fraud, despite denying all the allegations. His nomination for the Prix Goncourt was withdrawn.
So, who should we believe now — the author or the AI that claims to have identified AI-generated writing?
When the origins of texts become uncertain
"We will have to learn to live with doubt," says Hannes Bajohr, a professor of German literature at the University of California, Berkeley.

blocks.caption: Hannes Bajohr, professor for German Studies at the University of California, BerkeleyImage: Jen Siska

blocks.text: He has spent years examining how AI is changing both writing and reading. His prediction: If the origins of texts can no longer be reliably established, we will have to evaluate them differently. What matters will be their quality alone, rather than whether AI was used in the writing process.
Nina George, a best-selling author and honorary president of the European Writers' Council, is unwilling to accept this.
At the Frankfurt Book Fair, she was awarded the Friedrich Perthes Prize in recognition of her commitment to issues including AI and copyright.

blocks.caption: A leading advocate for European authors' rights and copyright reform: Author Nina GeorgeImage: Sabine Kieselbach/DW

blocks.text: George has addressed the European Parliament and the German Bundestag, and speaks and writes tirelessly about the dangers of AI models. It is perverse, she says, that an author should suddenly have to prove that their writing is human. The focus of her campaigning remains the large corporations' self-serving mentality and the protection of copyright.
Can anyone become an author with AI?
But what if an author sees AI not as an enemy, but as a tool that makes writing easier?
American author and artist Luke Stoffel deliberately used AI in his memoir, "How To Win One Million Dollars" and "Shit Glitter," and was open about doing so.
"I'm dyslexic," he says in a video interview. "I've always written and made up stories, but I never dared to take them any further."

blocks.caption: Luke Stoffel openly talks about his use of AI in writing booksImage: Privat

blocks.text: It was only with the help of AI, he says, that he was able to fulfill his dream. The technology drew his attention to weaknesses in his writing and suggested a marketing strategy that actually worked.
Then, in May 2026, he received an award from the Independent Book Publishers Association (IBPA) for the book.

For South African author Coral Hart, AI is actually the foundation of her business model. Publishing under various pseudonyms, she releases more than 200 different novels every year, spanning romance, thrillers and mystery, all independently published.

She sees herself as an ideas person, as well as an editor and publisher. Although none of her books has yet become a bestseller, the business is profitable. According to Hart, each of her books reaches more than 5,000 people.
Many publishers already working with AI

New York-based author Luke Stoffel considers the entire debate hypocritical. Many publishers have been working with AI tools for some time. He's certain that "right now, a million-copy bestseller is being printed that was created with the help of AI. The author won't admit it, and then there'll be a scandal."
It is entirely possible that the scandal surrounding Thélyson Orélien is precisely that story. But we may never know for sure.
For now, the battle against the tech giants continues. Even the companies themselves are increasingly concerned about losing control.

At the very start of the fair, the German Publishers and Booksellers Association issued an appeal to policymakers in Berlin and Brussels, calling for stricter regulation of artificial intelligence, more urgently than ever before. More than 150 publishers have already signed it.
But for now, it remains just an appeal. And the question of what authors themselves should be permitted to do with AI will undoubtedly continue to fuel debate in the future.
Reading 2.0: How AI is changing our books
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Banff is in Treaty 7 territory and leases its land from the feds. So what happens to it if Alberta separates?

image.caption: Hidden Lake in Banff National Park where researchers are reintroducing the native cutthroat trout near Lake Louise on Sept 1, 2022. The future of the federal parkland would be up in the air if Alberta were to separate from Canada. (Todd Korol/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: In the thousands of pages of negotiations that would surely result if Alberta were to secede from Canada, at least one chapter would likely be dedicated to the Town of Banff.

This tourist mecca is already a jurisdictional anomaly: situated on federal parkland that the town has leased for $550,000 a year since it incorporated in 1990. Residents own their homes but not their land; that's also leased from Ottawa.
The province operates the local hospital and schools, but the federal government has veto power over most bylaw changes.

In short, governance is complicated. And with Oct. 19 approaching — when Alberta will vote on, among other questions, whether to hold a referendum on separating from Canada — many of those who live in this mountain resort town are worried about the future.
The Town of Jasper, roughly 300 kilometres northwest of Banff, faces similar issues, given it's also based in a federal park in Alberta.
But it's the questions raised particularly in Banff, which has almost twice the population of Jasper, that indicate the scale of the seismic shift should a province secede.
What the Alberta separation debate means for Banff
Even if Albertans eventually voted to leave federation, they cannot legally do so without Canada's agreement, according to a 1998 Supreme Court decision that provides a framework on separation.

Negotiations over how to divide assets and debts could take years, according to political science professor Tom Urbaniak, based on the few comparables, such as the dissolution of Czechoslovakia or signing of the Nisga'a Agreement — which took a decade of negotiations between British Columbia and the involved First Nations.
"Separation means that everything is an open question," said Urbaniak, director of Cape Breton University's Tompkins Institute, adding that he hopes the concept remains hypothetical.

In Banff, the core questions are about belonging. Would Alberta — as Quebec separatists have asserted through the indivisibility principle — claim all land within its current borders, regardless of whether it is federal or provincial? What would it have to trade for Ottawa to agree?
Or would the town of roughly 8,000 people become a tiny piece of Canada isolated within a new country?

"This is what makes separation so perilous and, just from an objective perspective, so irresponsible [because it's not] a simplistic option," Urbaniak said. "The give and take of resources, payment of money, assumption of debt, renegotiation of treaties, compensation to the rest of Canada — all of this is on the table."
A plea from Banff's mayor
Banff's mayor has urged Albertans to vote against a referendum.
Ottawa has been a partner for decades, Corrie DiManno said, collaborating on major portfolios, including conservation management, wildfire prevention and housing.
The questions sparked by separation have created anxiety for her constituents, she said in a recent interview with CBC's The Sunday Magazine.
LISTEN | Banffites worry what might happen in a separate Alberta:
The Sunday Magazine24:34What would an independent Alberta mean for Canada's original national park?

DiManno keeps hearing from businesses worried about potential secession deterring visitors — last year, 4.5 million tourists went through Banff National Park — or what it might mean for those who live in Banff but work elsewhere in the Bow Valley.

"People have talked about, you know, am I going to need a passport to go to Canmore," she said, referring to another mountain hub a 20-minute drive southeast on Highway 1, but outside of the federal park.

"We really haven't had any formal conversations and, frankly, I really hope that we don't need to. I'm hoping that Albertans come out and finish this conversation once and for all to say that we will stay in Canada."

Banff Mayor Corrie DiManno is officially sworn in as a member of council during a swearing-in process on Oct. 28, 2025. DiManno is urging Albertans to keep the province in the federation. (Greg Colgan/CBC)
Her comments echo her May 25 Instagram post, which received widespread support — with hundreds of commenters thanking her for standing up for their community, for Alberta and for Canada.
In it, DiManno emphasized the law of the land runs deeper than municipal or provincial governance.

"Banff is on Treaty 7 territory and this treaty predates both Banff National Park and the province of Alberta," she said. "We all share a responsibility to respect the spirit and obligations of the treaties that created Canada."
A sacred place

For centuries, the Stoney Nakoda Nations have referred to Tunnel Mountain, which overlooks Banff on the town's eastern edge, as the Sacred Guardian Buffalo Mountain. The mountain and the area's hot springs are sacred to the surrounding Indigenous communities and are both included in the 149-year-old Treaty 7 agreement.

What that means is "not only would Indigenous nations have to have a seat at the table [in negotiations], if a treaty is being cancelled or significantly altered — but the consent of the affected Indigenous nations would be required for this all to be legal and constitutional," Urbaniak said.
A coalition of First Nations has already launched a legal challenge against the question of separation being put to a referendum.

items: First Nations' court challenge may block Alberta separatism itself, not just petition drive
First Nations in Alberta work to mobilize voters, prepare community members for referendum

blocks.text: The calls for separation to be put to a vote were initiated by the citizen group Stay Free Alberta, which claimed in the spring to have more than 177,800 signatures backing its push.

A judge annulled the petition in May, saying the province had failed in its duty to consult with First Nations. But Premier Danielle Smith then announced Alberta would appeal that decision and went ahead with the referendum on whether to hold a vote on separation.

Though Smith's office has since maintained it wants Alberta to remain in Canada, pundits have noted the decision to hold the referendum was made to appease hardline separatist factions in her voting base.
When asked about the premier's vision for Banff should Alberta separate, Smith's press secretary responded in an email that the United Conservative Party and caucus are committed to unity.
"We remain focused on our work to restore Albertans' hope in our country by building a stronger Alberta within a united Canada," Sam Blackett wrote in the statement.

Parks Canada did not directly answer questions about what would happen in the case of a separation, saying the federal government "respects the democratic process taking place in Alberta" and that it works "in collaboration with provinces, territories, Indigenous groups and communities" to protect "national historic sites and national parks."
'We are home'

Stoney Nakoda elder Alice Kaquitts scoffs at the idea of land ownership, noting that the area's First Nations have been part of Banff's stewards "since time immemorial" and have a deep and sacred connection to the area.

Kaquitts recalls how, as a girl, she and her parents would drive to Banff to sell crafts, with family pointing out landmarks and their connection to her culture along the route; how, as they drove into the park and the mountain rose up, her parents would pull over and get out of their vehicle to pray.
Stoney Nakoda Nations elder Alice Kaquitts says her people have been stewards of the Banff area since time immemorial. (Andrea Hoang/CBC)
"They would tell that sacred guardian, ‘We're home, we are home,'" she told The Sunday Magazine.
"That sacred connection to this area is something that I've never lost.… I can drown the town out, I can drown out urbanization in my mind, and I can hear my ancestors."
She notes the idea of land as a possession is a colonial concept and does not align with her traditional beliefs; instead, she believes in preserving a relationship with her natural surroundings.

items: Listen to The Sunday Magazine's roadtrip in the run-up to the referendum

blocks.text: It's why she is thankful, she said, that Indigenous leaders advanced the legal challenge against the question of separation.
"From a First Nations perspective, we viewed the treaties as a peace treaty — and what that entailed was 'We'll share the land with you,'" she said.
"That agreement was made with the Queen, not the province. We didn't sign a treaty with Alberta to give up this land."

articles.title: Art for freedom: Maria Kalesnikava in Bonn
articles.summary: The Belarusian musician and civil rights activist Maria Kalesnikava held the keynote speech on the importance of art at the 2026 Beethovenfest in Bonn. She also visited DW.

image.caption: Maria Kalesnikava continues to fight for freedom Image: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Maria Kalesnikava knows all too well how authoritarian regimes repress art: The Belarusian flautist and activist spent five years in detention as a political prisoner, three of which were in solitary confinement.

Speaking at this year's Beethovenfest, she said: "A person's external freedom can be taken away, sometimes almost entirely. Their freedom of movement, contacts with other people, and access to information can be limited." She pointed out that it is, however, much harder to control what has already become part of one's memory, imagination and inner experience. "And it is precisely in this that I find the explanation for why culture is so important for a free society and why authoritarian systems so often view it with distrust" she concluded during the keynote speech.

blocks.caption: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul welcomed Maria Kolesnikova at the Federal Foreign Office in December 2025Image: Amrei Schulz/AA/photothek.de/picture alliance

blocks.text: A key figure of the Belarusian opposition, the artist and political activist was arrested by the regime of Alexander Lukashenko in the summer of 2020, after the regime had violently suppressed the peaceful revolution for democracy and freedom. Across the country, mass protests and a democratic civil rights movement took place after the controversial presidential election on August 9, 2020.

Kalesnikava recalled how, during her imprisonment, she had carried her world and her experiences, with her all along. This enabled her to remain free, and not to feel like a victim. To Kalesnikava, this is precisely the power of art and also the reason why all dictators — whether Stalin, Hitler or Putin and Lukashenko — hate independent arts and culture, even if it's not overtly political.
During a panel discussion in Bonn, Kalesnikava stressed this point directly:

"The question often arises: what are we defending in Ukraine? Why do we need so much money and new weapons? For me, it is completely clear: the war Russia started is not just against Ukraine. It's a war against European values and European culture. It is a war against our civilization." Kalesnikava realized this immediately when she heard about the Russian war against Ukraine in February 2022, while she was imprisoned.
Music saved her

Kalesnikava was released and has been living in freedom again for ten months now — a miracle that she didn't think was possible and an achievement of international diplomacy. The fact that she emerged and returned to her life full of resilience is thanks in part to Beethoven and Bach, as Kalesnikava, who studied the flute and earned a degree in early and new music in Minsk and Stuttgart, recalled. "I spent a lot of time in complete silence. But this silence was almost never empty, because music constantly played in my head," Kalesnikava said in Bonn. "We musicians know this state very well — sometimes a melody or a musical phrase gets so stuck in your head that it's simply impossible to get rid of it. In normal life, this can even be annoying. In prison, I realized for the first time that this could bring great happiness."

blocks.caption: Maria Kolesnikova appeared on the Russian-language DW program "DW Novosti," on October 2, 2026Image: DW

blocks.text: During her visit to Bonn, the Belarusian activist also visited DW and appeared as a guest on the DW Russian language show "DW Novosti." Kalesnikava currently lives in Berlin following an invitation by the German government, where she is also recovering from the horrors she experienced. She sees it as her responsibility to remind the world about what is happening to more than 800 political prisoners in Belarus, as well as the importance and fragility of free artistic expression. On October 2, 2026, she held her keynote speech at the Beethovenfest in Bonn as part of a conference titled "Cultural Events as Political Spaces?," organized with the support of the German Federal Cultural Foundation.
The concert hall as a space for freedom

More than 200 representatives from concert institutions and music festivals from across Germany came to the newly renovated Beethovenhalle in Bonn for the final weekend of this year's Beethovenfest. Together, they debated innovative forms and formats for music, as well as issues that stretch far beyond the music industry and urge on to think outside the box.

blocks.caption: Steven Walter, artistic director of the Beethovenfest, spoke about the importance of music and freedom at the conference in BonnImage: Michael Staab/Beethovenfest

blocks.text: "Arts and culture are not responsible for taking on specific opinions from political parties, or for making explicitly political statements," Steven Walter, artistic director of the Beethovenfest and host of the conference, told DW. "What art always creates, however, is spaces for encounter, and places where people can tolerate ambivalence. And that is such an important part of our society, that we're able to handle making collective experiences." To Walter, this is precisely where arts and culture come in, as artists create spaces for independent thought, subjective interpretations, as well as doubts. "Perhaps it's true that there is something like a DNA of freedom in the nature of art," Walter explained in an interview with DW.
The most successful Beethovenfest in years

The festive closing of the 2026 Beethovenfest took place on 3 October, which is also German Unity Day. The BBC Philharmonic Orchestra, under the baton of conductor Anja Bihlmaier, performed Johannes Brahms' "A German Requiem," an iconic piece that evokes reconciliation and trust.

blocks.caption: At the closing concert of the Beethovenfest, Anja Bihlmaier conducted Brahms's Requiem with the BBC Philharmonic Orchestra and the Audi Youth Choir AcademyImage: Nekame Klasohm

blocks.text: After four weeks of Beethovenfest 2026, the festival recorded the highest number of visitors in a decade. Around 35,000 people came to experience, celebrate and discuss art together at more than 100 concerts and events.
This article was written by Andrey Gorezky, translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal and Tenzin Sekhon.

articles.title: What is your seafood eating? Investigation traces problems in global feed supply
articles.summary: Much of the fish meal and fish oil that support farmed salmon and imported seafood consumed in Canada come from global supply chains linked to pollution, labour abuses, overfishing, and food…

image.caption: Small fish like these Peruvian anchoveta are harvested from the wild to produce fish oil and fish meal that feeds aquaculture operations around the world. An investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project traces those global supply chains that are linked to pollution, labour abuses, overfishing, and food

blocks.text: The following story is part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, D.C.
In 2020, a team of government investigators in Goa, India, arrived at a factory named United Marine Products to find out how it was disposing of its toxic wastewater.

For years, local residents had complained that the factory was making their air unbreathable and their drinking water deadly. This factory produces fish meal, a protein-rich powder used to feed farmed fish, which is made by pulverizing and cooking wild-caught fish.

Soon enough, the inspectors discovered that the plant operators had employed a new and illegal way to dispose of the facility's wastewater, drilling bore holes into the ground in a field behind the plant. The authorities later concluded these holes likely contaminated groundwater and sickened villagers and livestock.

The United Marine Products plant in Councolim, Goa, India. In 2020, investigators determined the plant had drilled holes into the ground behind the plant to illegally dispose of wastewater from fish meal processing. (Changing Markets Foundation)
The plant owner denied wrongdoing.
Seafood consumers in Canada might think they have no connection to these sorts of far-away problems.

But this factory in India supplied Skretting, a major feed producer used by dozens of fish farms in Canada — so its product may feed the salmon from British Columbia and New Brunswick or trout from Quebec you see on store shelves.

A five-year investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, D.C., uncovered a variety of similar hidden costs involved in producing this feed, including the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths, and violent protests spurred by the horrid stench from fish meal factories.

These social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed, far from where the resulting luxury types of seafood are eaten.

A worker unloads a crate of anchovies from the holding area of a boat at the port of El Callao, Peru. The world’s largest producer of fishmeal, Peru faces growing concern about overfishing and pollution from its fishmeal industry. (Rodrigo Abd/The Associated Press)

Whether domestically raised or imported, the most popular types of farmed seafood consumed in Canada – salmon, shrimp, trout, sea bass, sea bream – are fed fish meal, which is made from the very kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion, say fisheries scientists.

“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at the University of B.C. in Vancouver.
“And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”
LISTEN | Stench, pollution and civil unrest: Ian Urbina unpacks the investigation:
The Current23:57The hidden costs of fish feed
Canada’s reliance on global fish meal

Since 2022, more than half of the seafood eaten globally has come from fish farms rather than wild catch, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization.
